ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Quiet interval after choking

A 20-month-old has a witnessed choking episode with severe coughing while eating a nut. The coughing settles, and he appears comfortable on arrival. His parents ask whether the quiet interval proves the nut was expelled. What is the best response?

  1. An asymptomatic interval can occur after an object lodges
  2. Settling cough confirms expulsion when oxygen saturation is normal
  3. A retained nut would necessarily produce immediate pneumonia
  4. Absence of stridor excludes an object in a bronchus
  5. An object still in the airway must remain visible on a plain radiograph
Answer and explanation

An asymptomatic interval can occur after an object lodges

Symptoms may temporarily lessen after the object lodges, so the initial event remains clinically important.

Option explanations

An asymptomatic interval can occur after an object lodges: Symptoms may temporarily lessen after the object lodges, so the initial event remains clinically important.

Settling cough confirms expulsion when oxygen saturation is normal: A partial obstruction may cause a quiet interval with normal oxygenation.

A retained nut would necessarily produce immediate pneumonia: Infectious complications can be delayed; immediate fever is not required.

Absence of stridor excludes an object in a bronchus: Stridor suggests proximal obstruction; a bronchial object may cause different or initially subtle findings.

An object still in the airway must remain visible on a plain radiograph: Many food objects are radiolucent, and a normal image does not prove clearance.
